history.heading: Governors of Thebes become kings
history.text:
The Eleventh Dynasty began as a family of provincial governors at Thebes in Upper Egypt, at a time when the country was divided. Its ancestor, Intef the Great, son of Iku, was a nomarch, a provincial governor, and never ruled as king; the first to be counted as a king is usually Mentuhotep I.

An inscription from the reign of Intef II shows that he was the first of the family to claim the rule of all Egypt. That claim brought the Thebans into conflict with the rival kings of the Tenth Dynasty at Herakleopolis in the north. Intef II campaigned northwards and took the important province of Abydos.

history.heading: Reunification under Mentuhotep II
history.text:
Warfare between Thebes and Herakleopolis continued on and off for decades, until the Herakleopolitans were defeated under Mentuhotep II, before the 39th year of his long reign. Egypt was united again, and his reign is taken as the beginning of the Middle Kingdom.

The Theban kings reasserted Egyptian influence abroad. Mentuhotep II sent expeditions to Phoenicia for cedar, and his successor Mentuhotep III sent an expedition from Coptos to the land of Punt.

history.heading: A mysterious ending
history.text:
Later records speak of "seven empty years" after the death of Mentuhotep III, which correspond to the reign of Mentuhotep IV, a king who was often left off later king lists. Almost the only thing known about his reign is that his vizier, Amenemhat, recorded two remarkable omens while leading an expedition to the quarries of the Wadi Hammamat.

Many scholars identify this vizier with Amenemhat I, the founder of the Twelfth Dynasty. How he came to the throne is not known; one theory is that he seized power in a palace coup.

history.heading: Many kings, one administration
history.text:
The Thirteenth Dynasty followed the Twelfth without an obvious break in government. Its kings at first continued to rule from Itjtawy, the Middle Kingdom capital near el-Lisht, and the administration built up by their predecessors kept working.

What makes the dynasty unusual is the number of its kings. Dozens of rulers are known, many of whom reigned for only a few years or even months, and the order of several of them is still uncertain. Much of the day-to-day continuity seems to have rested with the high officials, above all the viziers, rather than with the kings themselves.

history.heading: The best-known reigns
history.text:
A few kings reigned long enough to leave more substantial monuments. Neferhotep I and Sobekhotep IV, apparently brothers, are among the best attested, with inscriptions and statues from several sites in Egypt.

During the dynasty, royal control of the eastern Delta weakened, where communities of people from the Levant had grown in number. Later in the period the kings' authority was concentrated in the south, and Thebes became increasingly important.

history.heading: Into the Second Intermediate Period
history.text:
The end of the Thirteenth Dynasty is poorly understood. As its rulers lost hold of the north, other lines of kings arose in the Delta, among them the rulers known as the Hyksos, who would form the Fifteenth Dynasty. Egypt entered the Second Intermediate Period, a time when several dynasties ruled different parts of the country at once.

Because the sources are fragmentary, dates and reign lengths for this period vary between reference works; the dates on this site follow the conventional chronology and are approximate.

sources.label: I. Shaw (ed.), The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000): standard reference, chronology used on this site
Wikipedia, "Thirteenth Dynasty of Egypt" (for further reading)

history.heading: Kings at Thebes
history.text:
The Seventeenth Dynasty ruled from Thebes in Upper Egypt during the last decades of the Second Intermediate Period, while the Hyksos kings of the Fifteenth Dynasty held the north from their capital at Avaris. Its chronology is very uncertain and the later king lists help little, but most scholars regard it as a native Egyptian dynasty, founded by a king named Rahotep.

Under Hyksos supremacy the Theban kings revived the cult of Osiris, rebuilt temples and secured the religious centre of Abydos, the first steps towards reuniting the country.

history.heading: The war of liberation
history.text:
Open war began under Seqenenre Tao, who was killed in the fighting; the wounds on his mummy are among the most vivid evidence of the conflict. His son Kamose secured the south and then carried the war north against the Hyksos, but he died suddenly after only about two years on the throne.

Kamose left no sons. His younger brother Ahmose came to the throne as a boy of about ten.

history.heading: From Thebes to a united Egypt
history.text:
When he was old enough to lead the army, Ahmose took Memphis, captured the Hyksos capital with the help of the fleet, and pursued the Hyksos into southern Canaan, besieging their stronghold at Sharuhen for three years.

With that victory Ahmose reunited Upper and Lower Egypt. He is counted as the first king of the Eighteenth Dynasty, and his reign opens the New Kingdom.

sources.label: Wikipedia, "Seventeenth Dynasty of Egypt" (reference work consulted)
I. Shaw (ed.), The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000): chronology used on this site

history.heading: Setnakhte and Ramesses III
history.text:
The Twentieth Dynasty was the last of the New Kingdom. It began after a period of civil war at the end of the Nineteenth Dynasty, recorded on a stela at Elephantine set up by Setnakhte, who restored order and founded the new line. He reigned only a few years and was succeeded by his son Ramesses III.

Ramesses III faced the great crisis of the age. The movements of the Sea Peoples were part of the collapse of the Late Bronze Age world, in which the Hittite empire disappeared. Ramesses defeated Libyan invasions in his 5th and 11th years and, in his 8th year, a confederacy of Sea Peoples on land and at sea. His mortuary temple at Medinet Habu records these wars.

history.heading: Strikes, conspiracy and robbery
history.text:
Strain soon showed. In Ramesses III's 29th year the royal tomb builders of Deir el-Medina stopped work when their rations failed to arrive, the first recorded strike in history. His reign ended with a harem conspiracy to put his son Pentawer on the throne; the plot killed the king, but his heir Ramesses IV succeeded and had the conspirators tried.

Ramesses IV began ambitious building works and sent large expeditions to the Wadi Hammamat. Under his successors, the workmen were repeatedly kept from work by fear of Libyan raiders. In the 16th and 17th years of Ramesses IX, investigations into tomb robbery at Thebes found that many tombs had been broken into.

history.heading: Priests and the end of the New Kingdom
history.text:
The tomb of Ramesses VI, cut into the Valley of the Kings, buried the entrance of Tutankhamun's tomb under its debris and so kept it safe until 1922. Meanwhile, documents such as the Wilbour Papyrus show how much land and wealth was controlled by the temple of Amun.

Droughts, low Nile floods, famine, unrest and quarrels among the heirs of Ramesses III weakened the kings further. Under Ramesses XI, the High Priests of Amun were effectively rulers of the south, while Smendes controlled the north. After Ramesses XI's death, Smendes founded the Twenty-first Dynasty at Tanis.

sources.label: Wikipedia, "Twentieth Dynasty of Egypt" (reference work consulted)

history.heading: Kings at Tanis, priests at Thebes
history.text:
The Twenty-first Dynasty opened the Third Intermediate Period. Its founder, Smendes, had already controlled Lower Egypt under the last Ramesside king. The new kings ruled from Tanis in the north-eastern Delta, which is why the dynasty is called Tanite, but their power was effective mainly in Lower Egypt.

In Middle and Upper Egypt, the High Priests of Amun at Thebes governed in all but name, while still recognising the kings at Tanis.

history.heading: Royal tombs at Tanis
history.text: The kings of the dynasty were buried inside the temple enclosure at Tanis. The tombs found there in the 20th century, including that of Psusennes I with its precious burial equipment, are among the richest royal burials known from Egypt, although they are far less famous than Tutankhamun's.

history.heading: Saving the New Kingdom kings
history.text:
In Thebes, the priests faced the consequences of the tomb robberies of the late New Kingdom. They gathered the mummies of many earlier kings from their plundered tombs in the Valley of the Kings, rewrapped them and reburied them together in hidden caches, such as the one at Deir el-Bahari found in 1881, which held the mummy of Seti I among others.

Manetho gives the dynasty a length of 130 years. It was followed by the kings of Libyan descent of the Twenty-second Dynasty.

sources.label: Wikipedia, "Twenty-first Dynasty of Egypt" (reference work consulted)
